subtitle: Download, save, switch it off and on again
words.intro: Germany builds very good machines, and it explains them in very long manuals. When something breaks, you call a hotline, and a calm voice asks you to turn it off and on again.

grammar[0].fact: Many IT words in German are English with a German coat on: *downloaden, ich habe gedownloadet*. Purists prefer *herunterladen*. Both are in the dictionary. A *Handy* is not an English word at all, whatever Germans believe.

grammar[1].blocks[1].title: At the hotline
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: *Das hat nichts gebracht*: it was no use. A very useful sentence.
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Spell it
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: They will ask for your customer number, and your name letter by letter. On the phone Germans use names: *A wie Anton, D wie Dora, M wie Martha*. Learn your own name that way once.
grammar[1].fact: The German telephone alphabet was reformed in 2022: it now uses city names, *A wie Aachen, B wie Berlin*, to replace first names, some of which had been changed by the Nazis to remove Jewish ones. Nearly everyone still says Anton and Berta.

document.intro: A real instruction label from an Austrian chemist, more than a hundred years old. *Gebrauchsanweisung* is a word you still see on everything you buy. The medicine is for horses. Read how instructions used to be written, with *man*.
document.fact: German instructions are famously thorough. The law requires them to be in German, and the ones for simple things can run to dozens of pages. *Gebrauchsanweisung lesen* is what your German friend will suggest before helping.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Turn each line into an instruction to a stranger, with Sie.
reading.intro: Maya’s laptop has died the night before a deadline. She rings the hotline. She has been on hold for 47 minutes, with the same twelve bars of music, and now a human voice is on the line. It is called Herr Dörr.
reading.photos[0].caption: Der Motor funktioniert nicht. Haben Sie ihn schon aus- und eingeschaltet?
reading.fact: Germans are cautious about data: *Datenschutz*, data protection, is taken very seriously. Many still pay in cash, and when street-view photos arrived, hundreds of thousands of owners had their houses blurred.
